reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 5, Reasoning with SQL Logic. In the earlier modules, we focused on retrieving data, changing data safely, and creating summaries. Now we are moving into something that looks simple at first, but becomes very important in real projects: deciding which rows qualify and how each row should be interpreted.

Think about a real system. A hospital may need to identify patients who are active, have given consent, have a high-risk diagnosis, and do not have usable contact information. A university may need to find students who are enrolled, have not completed a requirement, and either have a low grade or a missing assignment. A business may want customers who are active, have not purchased recently, and are eligible for a promotion. These are not just filtering problems. They are decision rules.

[tts-break]

In this module, we will work with AND, OR, and NOT, but we will also go deeper into SQL's treatment of missing values. SQL does not always produce only true or false. When NULL is involved, a condition can become UNKNOWN. That one idea explains many SQL results that surprise beginners.

We will also use tools such as IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, COALESCE, NULLIF, and CASE. The goal is not to memorize a list of keywords. The goal is to develop a reasoning process. Before writing SQL, state the rule in plain language. Decide what missing data means. Then write the condition and test edge cases. If you can explain why every row was included, excluded, or classified, then your SQL is doing more than running correctly; it is representing the rule correctly.

slides.title: Big picture
slides.transcript:
Module 4 focused heavily on aggregation. We asked questions such as: how many admissions occurred, what is the average bill amount, or how many records belong to each category? Module 5 asks a different kind of question: which rule applies to each row?

Suppose a company is building a customer-retention campaign. The business rule might say: include customers who are active, who have agreed to receive messages, and who either have not purchased in ninety days or have recently submitted a complaint. Notice how quickly the logic becomes layered. We have AND connecting required conditions, OR connecting alternatives, and possibly missing values for consent, purchase dates, or complaint status.

[tts-break]

The same thing happens in healthcare. A patient may qualify for follow-up only when the patient is active, consent is explicitly true, the diagnosis belongs to a target group, and there is no usable email address. If consent is NULL, should that be treated as false? Maybe not. It may mean consent has never been recorded, which could require manual review.

This is why SQL logic should start from the policy, not from the syntax. We will repeatedly use the same process: write the rule in plain English, identify fields that may be missing, group related conditions clearly, test boundary cases, and then compare the result with the original rule.

A query can be perfectly valid SQL and still be analytically wrong. In this module, we are training ourselves to catch those quiet logic errors.

slides.title: Learning objectives
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, I want you to be comfortable doing more than writing a WHERE clause. You should be able to look at a written business rule and translate it into SQL while being able to explain why the result is correct.

You will practice combining Boolean conditions using AND, OR, and NOT. You will learn how SQL's three-valued logic works, meaning that expressions can evaluate to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. You will see why NULL requires special treatment and why ordinary comparisons such as equals NULL do not work the way beginners often expect.

We will also use NULL-safe tools. IS NULL and IS NOT NULL let us test missingness directly. IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN are useful for nullable Boolean fields. IS DISTINCT FROM gives us a definite comparison even when NULL is involved. COALESCE provides fallback values, and NULLIF helps normalize special values such as blank text or zero denominators.

[tts-break]

Another major objective is learning CASE expressions. CASE allows us to turn rules into labels such as High Risk, Standard, Needs Review, or No Charge. But CASE is order-sensitive. The first true branch wins, so broad conditions can accidentally hide more specific ones.

Finally, I want you to validate your logic. Test NULL, zero, blank text, exact thresholds, and overlapping conditions. In a real project, those edge cases are often where the most expensive mistakes happen.

slides.title: Six-step workflow
slides.transcript:
This six-step workflow is the pattern I want you to reuse throughout the module.

First, state the rule in plain language. Before writing SQL, you should be able to explain the requirement to another person. For example: select active patients who have explicitly consented and who have either Diabetes or Kidney Disease.

Second, identify which fields can be missing. If consent can be NULL, decide whether NULL means no, unknown, or needs review. That decision should come from the business meaning, not from convenience.

Third, group related conditions with parentheses. This is especially important when AND and OR appear together. Parentheses make your intention visible and reduce the chance that operator precedence changes the meaning.

[tts-break]

Fourth, if you are using CASE, place the most specific or highest-priority branches first. Remember that CASE stops at the first true branch.

Fifth, test edge cases. Try exact threshold values, such as exactly sixty-five years old. Test zero. Test NULL. Test empty text and text that contains only spaces. Test a row that satisfies more than one condition.

Finally, compare the output with the written rule. Do not stop at “the query ran.” Ask whether every important row behaves as expected.

You can use this workflow outside SQL too. It is essentially a small decision-modeling process: define the policy, identify uncertainty, encode the logic, test the boundaries, and validate the result.

slides.title: Practice schema
slides.transcript:
For this module, we use a small synthetic healthcare database. The data is intentionally simple enough to understand, but it contains the kinds of messy values that create real logic problems.

The patient information table includes demographics, contact fields, activity status, consent, and preferred language. The diagnostics table contains diagnosis, severity, and confirmation information. Patient billing contains bill amounts, payments, and payment status. Admissions gives us admission and discharge dates.

There is also a convenience view called patient_case. That view combines information from several source tables so we can focus on logic rather than spending the whole module on joins. We will return to joins in the next module.

[tts-break]

What makes this dataset useful is the edge cases. Some values are NULL. Some text values are empty. Some contain only spaces. One bill amount is exactly zero. One payment status is missing. One consent value is unknown.

Those are not random annoyances. They are the records that help us understand whether our rule is actually robust.

Imagine a production system where an email field contains a space because someone pressed the spacebar and saved the form. A simple IS NULL test would say that email exists, even though there is no usable address. Or imagine a zero-dollar bill that represents a waived charge. Treating it as missing would be incorrect.

So as we work, think of this database as a controlled laboratory for learning how real-world data behaves.

slides.title: Boolean logic map
slides.transcript:
AND, OR, and NOT are the basic building blocks of SQL decision rules.

AND means that every connected condition must be satisfied. If a customer must be active and have a balance above a threshold, both conditions need to be true.

OR means that at least one alternative can qualify. A student might need support if the student has a low exam score or has missed multiple assignments. Either condition is enough.

NOT reverses a known condition. For example, we may want records that are active but not already completed.

That sounds straightforward, but SQL adds one more truth state: UNKNOWN. This usually appears when a comparison involves NULL.

[tts-break]

It helps to think about these operators in terms of cohort size. AND usually makes a group smaller because each additional requirement removes rows. OR usually makes a group larger because more alternatives can qualify. NOT can exclude a group, but when the underlying expression is UNKNOWN, NOT does not magically turn it into TRUE. NOT UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN.

A useful real-world example is a loan-review rule. Suppose the rule requires income above a threshold and verified identity. If identity verification is missing, the system cannot honestly say the condition is true. It also may not be correct to say it is false. SQL represents that uncertainty as UNKNOWN.

This is why Boolean logic in SQL is not only about syntax. It is about how certain or uncertain information affects decisions.

slides.title: AND
slides.transcript:
AND means every connected condition must be true.

In the example on this slide, a record must be active, the patient's age must be at least forty, and the severity must be High. If any one of those conditions is false, that row does not qualify.

When you run the query, do not just look at the rows that remain. Also think about the rows that disappeared. Maybe one patient is active and older than forty but has Medium severity. That row fails because AND requires all three parts.

A useful habit is to read the WHERE clause as a sentence. Say: I want patients who are active AND are at least forty AND have High severity. If the sentence sounds like all conditions are required at the same time, AND is the natural connector.

[tts-break]

This appears constantly in real projects. A university may select students who are currently enrolled AND have completed prerequisites AND have no registration hold. An e-commerce system may offer a promotion only to customers who are active AND belong to a certain region AND have a minimum purchase history.

One important point: adding another AND condition usually narrows the result. If you add a fourth requirement and your result becomes larger, that is a signal to inspect the logic.

Before running a complex AND rule, predict at least one record that should qualify and one that should not. That simple habit makes debugging much easier.

slides.title: OR
slides.transcript:
OR represents alternatives. A row remains when at least one condition is true.

In this slide, a patient qualifies when the diagnosis is Pneumonia, Flu, or Asthma. The patient does not need to have all three diagnoses. Any one of those values is enough.

If several OR conditions compare the same column with a set of values, IN can often make the rule easier to read. Instead of repeating diagnosis equals Pneumonia OR diagnosis equals Flu OR diagnosis equals Asthma, we can say diagnosis IN this list.

[tts-break]

Think about a customer-service project. A case may be considered urgent if the customer is a VIP, OR the complaint is about fraud, OR the issue has been open for more than forty-eight hours. Different paths can lead to the same outcome.

OR often broadens the result. If one condition returns ten rows and you add another OR condition, the combined result will normally contain the original rows plus any new rows that satisfy the second condition.

The challenge begins when OR and AND are mixed. For example, active AND high risk OR senior. Does active apply to both groups or only to high risk? That depends on grouping and operator precedence.

So OR by itself is simple. The important skill is recognizing which conditions are alternatives and making those alternatives visually clear when the rule becomes more complex.

slides.title: NOT
slides.transcript:
NOT negates a Boolean expression. If an expression is TRUE, NOT makes it FALSE. If it is FALSE, NOT makes it TRUE.

On this slide, we keep active records while excluding selected diagnoses. We can think of it as: the patient must be active, and the diagnosis must not belong to this excluded group.

Parentheses help make the target of NOT obvious. We are not negating one value. We are negating the whole membership test.

But there is an important SQL detail: NOT does not eliminate uncertainty. If an expression is UNKNOWN because it involves NULL, then NOT UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN.

[tts-break]

Imagine a retail table with a membership status that can be Gold, Silver, Basic, or NULL. If we ask for NOT Gold using an ordinary comparison, the NULL row does not automatically become “not Gold.” SQL does not know whether that missing value might actually have been Gold. The result can remain UNKNOWN.

This matters because WHERE keeps only TRUE rows.

So when you write NOT, ask two questions. First, what exact condition am I negating? Second, can any values involved be NULL?

Sometimes a more explicit predicate such as IS DISTINCT FROM communicates the rule better than a negated ordinary comparison. We will see that later. The main idea is to avoid treating missing information as if it were known information.

slides.title: Operator precedence
slides.transcript:
SQL has rules for deciding which logical operators are evaluated first. In PostgreSQL, NOT has higher precedence than AND, and AND has higher precedence than OR.

That means an expression like A OR B AND C is interpreted as A OR the combination of B AND C. SQL does not automatically read it the way a human might casually read the sentence.

You could memorize that order, and it is useful to know it, but I do not recommend relying on memory when writing important logic. Parentheses are much safer.

[tts-break]

Suppose a scholarship rule says a student qualifies when the student has a GPA above 3.5 OR belongs to a special program, AND the student has submitted the required form. If we do not group the conditions, the form requirement may apply only to the special-program branch. Students with high GPA could qualify even without the form.

That may be exactly what the policy intends, or it may be completely wrong.

Parentheses make the decision explicit. They also help the next analyst who reads the query months later. Think of parentheses as documentation, not just syntax.

My recommendation for this course is simple: whenever AND and OR appear in the same rule, group the conditions in a way that mirrors the plain-language requirement. You should not need to mentally calculate precedence just to understand a business rule.

slides.title: Parentheses change the rule
slides.transcript:
This slide shows why parentheses are part of the meaning of a query.

We have two versions of a rule. In the first version, because AND is evaluated before OR, the consent condition applies only to the Kidney Disease branch. That means anyone who satisfies the age condition can qualify even when consent is false.

In the second version, parentheses group the age condition and the Kidney Disease condition together. Then the consent requirement is applied to the whole group. Now consent is required regardless of which alternative caused the patient to qualify.

[tts-break]

The patient Lisa Ray is a useful boundary example because she is older than sixty-five but has false consent. In the unparenthesized rule, her age is enough to qualify. In the parenthesized rule, she fails because consent is required for both alternatives.

This is not a tiny formatting difference. Imagine this were a real outreach campaign. The first query could include people who explicitly declined contact. That could create a privacy or compliance problem even though the SQL contains no syntax error.

When you see a rule such as “A or B, but only when C is true,” write it as a grouped expression: the A-or-B portion belongs together, and then C applies to that whole decision.

Run both versions and compare the output. Seeing one record move in or out makes the precedence rule much easier to remember.

slides.title: Three-valued logic
slides.transcript:
SQL does not operate only with TRUE and FALSE. When NULL is involved, SQL can produce a third state called UNKNOWN.

NULL is not a value such as zero, false, or an empty string. It represents missing, unknown, or sometimes not-applicable information. Because SQL does not know the underlying value, many ordinary comparisons cannot be evaluated as definitely true or definitely false.

Suppose a patient's age is NULL. If we ask whether age is greater than sixty-five, SQL cannot say yes, because the value is missing. But it also cannot say no, because the real age could be seventy. The result is UNKNOWN.

[tts-break]

The most important practical rule is that WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE. FALSE is removed, and UNKNOWN is also removed.

This can make rows disappear in ways that surprise people. A customer with a missing subscription status may vanish from both “status equals Active” and “status not equal Active” queries, because neither comparison is definitely true.

In a real data-quality workflow, UNKNOWN is often meaningful. Missing consent might mean “needs review.” Missing payment status might mean “investigate.” Missing diagnosis confirmation might mean “pending.”

So do not think of UNKNOWN as an error. Think of it as SQL honestly saying: based on the information available, I cannot prove this condition either way.

slides.title: Truth table
slides.transcript:
Three-valued logic becomes easier when we reason through a few combinations instead of trying to memorize a large truth table.

Take TRUE AND UNKNOWN. The final result is UNKNOWN. We know one side is true, but the unknown side could still be false, so the whole expression cannot be guaranteed true.

Now take FALSE AND UNKNOWN. That result is definitely FALSE. Once one side of an AND condition is false, the whole expression cannot become true regardless of the missing side.

For OR, TRUE OR UNKNOWN is definitely TRUE because one true condition is enough. FALSE OR UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN because the missing side could still turn the expression into true.

And NOT UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN.

[tts-break]

Here is a practical way to think about it. Ask whether the known information is already enough to determine the outcome.

If an online order is already marked fraudulent, then “fraudulent OR missing address verification” is still true. We do not need the second condition to know the answer.

If a patient is definitely inactive, then “active AND unknown consent” is definitely false. The missing consent cannot rescue the rule.

When you run the truth-table example, focus less on memorizing every cell and more on asking: is the known side enough to settle the decision? That reasoning scales better when conditions become more complex.

slides.title: WHERE keeps only TRUE
slides.transcript:
This slide focuses on one rule that explains many SQL surprises: WHERE keeps only TRUE.

The example contains three Boolean states: true, false, and NULL. When we use the Boolean field directly in a WHERE clause, only the true row remains.

The false row is excluded, which feels natural. The NULL row is also excluded because NULL behaves as UNKNOWN. SQL cannot prove that the condition is true.

[tts-break]

Now think about a nullable consent field. If we write WHERE consent, only patients with explicit true consent remain. Patients with false consent are removed, and patients with unknown consent are also removed.

That may be exactly what we want for a messaging campaign, because we should not assume permission when consent has not been recorded.

But imagine a data-quality report whose purpose is to find anyone who has not explicitly consented. In that case, false and NULL may both be important. A simple WHERE consent would not answer that question.

The lesson is that WHERE has a very strict gate: only TRUE passes. Before filtering on a nullable condition, decide what you want to do with unknown values. Exclude them, include them, or label them separately. Make that policy explicit instead of letting SQL choose it accidentally.

slides.title: Why = NULL fails
slides.transcript:
A very common beginner mistake is writing equals NULL when trying to find missing values.

The problem is conceptual. Equality compares two known values. NULL means the value is unknown. Asking whether something equals an unknown value does not produce a definite answer. Even when the column itself is NULL, SQL does not say TRUE. It says UNKNOWN.

The same problem occurs with not equal NULL. SQL still cannot prove the relationship.

That is why SQL gives us special predicates: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

[tts-break]

Think about a form where an emergency contact has never been entered. We are not asking whether the contact value is literally equal to some value called NULL. We are asking whether there is no known value stored. IS NULL expresses that question directly.

Run the example and look at the calculated comparisons. You will see NULL results rather than useful true-or-false answers when ordinary equality is used.

This is one of those SQL habits worth learning early and keeping forever: if your question is about missingness, use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

Do not use equals NULL, and do not use not-equal NULL. Even if the syntax is accepted, the logic will not give the result you probably intend.

slides.title: Missing versus blank text
slides.transcript:
Missing text and blank text are not the same thing in PostgreSQL.

NULL means no known value. An empty string is a real text value containing zero characters. A string made only of spaces is also a real value until those spaces are removed.

This matters when the business rule says something like “the patient has no usable email address.”

If we test only email IS NULL, we will miss an empty string. We will also miss a value that contains three spaces. From the user's perspective, all three may mean “no usable email,” but the database sees them differently.

[tts-break]

A useful normalization pattern is to trim the text first. BTRIM removes leading and trailing whitespace. Then NULLIF compares that cleaned value with an empty string. If they are equal, NULLIF returns NULL. After that, IS NULL can treat missing, empty, and whitespace-only values consistently.

This pattern appears outside healthcare all the time. Customer phone fields, product descriptions, survey comments, usernames, and address lines can all contain blank-looking values that are technically not NULL.

The deeper lesson is to separate storage representation from business meaning. The database may store three different technical forms, while your analytical rule may want to treat them as one concept: “not usable.”

slides.title: Boolean predicates
slides.transcript:
A Boolean column can have three meaningful states when NULL is allowed: true, false, and unknown.

Consider a consent field. TRUE may mean the person explicitly agreed. FALSE may mean the person explicitly declined. NULL may mean nobody has recorded a decision yet.

Those are three different business states, and treating NULL as if it were FALSE can destroy that distinction.

PostgreSQL gives us predicates such as IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN. These make the intention very clear.

[tts-break]

Imagine an approval workflow. approved IS TRUE means approval was explicitly granted. approved IS FALSE means it was explicitly rejected. approved IS UNKNOWN means a decision has not been recorded.

That is much more informative than simply saying approved or NOT approved.

Run the example and inspect the patient whose consent is NULL. The explicit-yes flag should be false, the explicit-no flag should also be false, and the not-recorded flag should be true.

This is particularly important in domains where the difference between “no” and “we do not know” matters, such as privacy consent, legal approval, eligibility review, identity verification, or clinical confirmation.

When a Boolean column is nullable, do not automatically think of it as a two-state switch. Ask what the third state means in the real process.

slides.title: IS DISTINCT FROM
slides.transcript:
IS DISTINCT FROM is one of PostgreSQL's most useful NULL-safe comparison tools.

Ordinary equality and inequality can produce UNKNOWN when NULL is involved. IS DISTINCT FROM always gives a definite true-or-false answer.

If two known values are equal, they are not distinct. If two known values are different, they are distinct. If both values are NULL, PostgreSQL treats them as not distinct for this comparison. If one is NULL and the other is a known value, they are distinct.

There is also IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, which behaves like NULL-safe equality.

[tts-break]

Suppose you are comparing yesterday's customer profile with today's profile to identify changes. If both phone numbers are NULL, you probably do not want to mark that as a change. Ordinary comparisons make that awkward because NULL introduces UNKNOWN. IS DISTINCT FROM lets you say: tell me whether these two fields are meaningfully different, including their missingness.

Another example is a payment status rule. If you want everything that is not definitely Paid, a missing status should count as different from Paid. IS DISTINCT FROM expresses that clearly.

Use this tool when NULL is part of the comparison itself and you want a definite Boolean result instead of UNKNOWN.

slides.title: COALESCE
slides.transcript:
COALESCE provides fallback logic. PostgreSQL evaluates the expressions from left to right and returns the first one that is not NULL.

A common example is contact information. We may prefer email first, then mobile phone, then home phone, and finally a text label such as No contact provided.

But there is an important detail: COALESCE only understands NULL. It does not know that an empty string or a few spaces are useless contact information. If email contains a blank string, COALESCE may stop there and return that blank value instead of moving to the mobile number.

That is why COALESCE is often paired with normalization using BTRIM and NULLIF.

[tts-break]

COALESCE also appears in numeric work, but you need to be careful with meaning. Replacing a missing amount with zero is not just a technical operation. It makes a business assumption that missing means none.

For example, if amount_paid is NULL because no payment was made, zero may be reasonable. But if the amount is NULL because the payment system failed to load data, replacing it with zero could be misleading.

So the rule is not “use COALESCE whenever you see NULL.” The rule is “use COALESCE when the fallback value has a clear, documented meaning.”

slides.title: NULLIF
slides.transcript:
NULLIF is a small function with many practical uses.

It compares two expressions. If they are equal, it returns NULL. Otherwise, it returns the first expression.

For text cleaning, a useful pattern is to trim a field and then compare it with an empty string. If the cleaned text is empty, NULLIF converts it to NULL. This allows us to treat empty and whitespace-only text as missing.

For example, a preferred-language field might contain three spaces because a user clicked into the field and saved without typing anything. After trimming, that becomes an empty string. NULLIF can turn it into NULL so later logic becomes simpler.

[tts-break]

NULLIF is also useful when a particular numeric value should be treated specially. The classic example is a denominator of zero. NULLIF can convert exactly zero to NULL before division, preventing a division-by-zero error.

What I like about NULLIF is that it makes the rule visible. We are saying: if this value equals a particular sentinel or invalid value, treat it as missing for this calculation.

It is not a universal cleaning function. Use it when two values being equal should intentionally produce NULL.

slides.title: Normalize then fall back
slides.transcript:
This slide combines two ideas: normalize messy text first, then apply fallback logic.

Suppose our contact priority is email first, then mobile phone, then home phone, and finally No contact provided.

If we feed raw fields directly into COALESCE, an email containing only spaces may be treated as available because it is technically not NULL. That would block the fallback even though the email is unusable.

So each contact field is cleaned first. We trim the text. Then NULLIF converts an empty cleaned value to NULL. Only after that do we use COALESCE.

[tts-break]

This creates a very natural pipeline: standardize what “missing” means, then choose the first usable value.

Run the query and inspect the edge cases. Some patients should fall back from email to mobile or home phone. A patient with no usable contact values should receive the final display label.

You can use the same pattern in many projects. A shipping system may choose primary address, then secondary address. A customer profile may prefer work email, then personal email. A product catalog may prefer official description, then short description, then a placeholder.

The order inside COALESCE is not merely technical. It represents business priority. That priority should be chosen intentionally.

slides.title: Safe ratios with NULLIF
slides.transcript:
NULLIF is especially useful when calculating ratios because division by zero is an error.

Suppose we calculate percent paid as amount paid divided by bill amount. Most rows work normally, but one record has a bill amount of exactly zero because the service was categorized as No Charge.

Dividing by zero does not make analytical sense, and PostgreSQL will not allow it. By using NULLIF on the denominator, we say: if bill amount equals zero, treat the denominator as NULL for this calculation. Division by NULL returns NULL instead of raising an error.

[tts-break]

That NULL result has a useful meaning: this percentage is not computable for a zero-dollar bill. It is not the same as zero percent paid.

The numerator in the example may use COALESCE to treat missing amount paid as zero. Notice that this is a different decision. One function handles an invalid denominator; the other applies a fallback assumption to the numerator.

This pattern appears in many domains: click-through rate, defect rate, utilization rate, conversion rate, mortality rate, or average cost per event. Any denominator can potentially be zero.

Safe SQL does not merely prevent crashes. It preserves the meaning of the calculation while making exceptional cases visible.

slides.title: CASE mental model
slides.transcript:
CASE lets us create derived values based on rules. You can think of it as a decision tree written inside SQL.

PostgreSQL evaluates the WHEN branches from top to bottom. As soon as one condition is true, CASE returns that branch's result and stops checking the later branches for that row.

That makes branch order part of the logic.

Suppose we are labeling support tickets. If the first branch says response time greater than one hour equals Delayed, and a later branch says response time greater than twenty-four hours equals Critical, the Critical branch will never run because every ticket above twenty-four hours already satisfies the broader one-hour condition.

[tts-break]

The safer order is usually specific before broad, or highest priority before lower priority.

CASE can also include ELSE. ELSE gives a default result when no WHEN condition matches. If ELSE is omitted, PostgreSQL returns NULL.

Before writing a CASE expression, I recommend listing the categories in plain language and checking for overlap. Ask: can one row satisfy more than one branch? If yes, which result should win?

CASE is powerful because it allows business logic to become visible directly in a query. But that also means poorly ordered branches can encode the wrong policy while still producing valid-looking output.

slides.title: Searched CASE
slides.transcript:
Searched CASE is the flexible form of CASE because every WHEN contains a complete Boolean condition.

That makes it ideal for ranges, multiple-field rules, NULL checks, and complicated classifications.

In the billing example, we handle NULL first. That is important because a missing bill should not quietly fall into the Low-Value category. Then we check the highest threshold, followed by the next threshold, and finally use ELSE for the remaining known amounts.

Read the logic like a decision tree: if the bill is missing, label it Unknown. Otherwise, if it is at least the high-value threshold, label it High-Value. Otherwise, if it is at least the standard threshold, label it Standard. Otherwise, label it Low-Value.

[tts-break]

This same structure can classify students by risk level, customers by spending tier, patients by severity, or servers by CPU utilization.

When ranges are involved, pay attention to exact boundaries. If High-Value starts at ten thousand, then exactly ten thousand belongs there. If Standard starts at five thousand, then exactly five thousand belongs in Standard.

Run the query and inspect NULL, zero, and threshold values. Boundary testing is how we confirm that the written rule and the SQL rule are the same.

slides.title: Simple CASE
slides.transcript:
Simple CASE is useful when one expression needs to be mapped to a set of exact values.

For example, payment status can be Paid, No Charge, Open, Pending Review, or something else. We can compare that one field against each expected value and return a corresponding action.

Paid and No Charge may map to Closed. Open may map to Follow up. Pending Review may map to Investigate. Anything else can fall to ELSE.

This is similar to a lookup table written directly inside the query.

[tts-break]

Simple CASE is clean when the rule is truly based on exact values. It is less suitable for conditions such as amount greater than five thousand, age above sixty-five, or status is missing AND severity is High. Those are better expressed with searched CASE.

A practical example is converting coded values to readable labels. A university system might map A to Active, G to Graduated, and W to Withdrawn. A support system might map ticket codes to display categories.

Notice what happens when payment status is NULL. NULL does not match the named values, so the ELSE branch becomes important. In this example, ELSE can label it Status missing.

Choose simple CASE when you are mapping one field's exact values. Choose searched CASE when the rule itself contains conditions.

slides.title: CASE branch order
slides.transcript:
CASE branch order becomes critical when conditions overlap.

Suppose we want to label people as Senior when age is at least sixty-five and Adult when age is at least eighteen.

If we check age greater than or equal to eighteen first, a seventy-year-old patient matches that branch immediately. CASE stops and returns Adult. The Senior branch is never reached.

The correct order is to place the more specific or higher threshold first: check for Senior, then Adult.

[tts-break]

This same mistake appears in many real systems. A fraud score above ninety might be Critical, while a score above fifty is Review. If the Review condition comes first, the Critical category disappears. A bill above ten thousand may be High-Value, while above five thousand is Standard. High-Value needs to come first.

A useful test is to ask whether one condition logically contains another. Every value above ten thousand is also above five thousand. Every senior adult is also an adult.

When one condition contains another, the narrower condition usually belongs first.

Run both versions and compare older patients. You are not just learning CASE syntax here. You are learning how order can encode priority.

slides.title: Boundary-safe billing tiers
slides.transcript:
A good classification rule should make its boundaries easy to explain.

In the billing example, we first handle NULL as Unknown. Then bills of ten thousand or more are High-Value. Bills of five thousand or more, but below ten thousand, are Standard. Remaining known values are Low-Value.

Because we write the thresholds from high to low, we do not need to manually state an upper bound on the Standard branch. If the amount were ten thousand or more, it would already have matched High-Value.

[tts-break]

Boundary testing is essential. Ask what happens at exactly ten thousand. It should be High-Value. What happens at exactly five thousand? It should be Standard. What happens at four thousand nine hundred ninety-nine? Low-Value.

Later, we add a No Charge category for exactly zero. That is a good example of domain knowledge changing the rule. Zero is technically less than five thousand, so without a special branch it would be labeled Low-Value. But in the business context, No Charge communicates a different meaning.

Whenever you create tiers, write down the threshold values and test directly on those boundaries. Most classification bugs happen near edges, not in the obvious middle cases.

slides.title: Missing ELSE
slides.transcript:
If a CASE expression has no ELSE and none of the WHEN conditions match, PostgreSQL returns NULL.

Sometimes that is exactly what you want. NULL might mean unclassified or not applicable. But other times it creates ambiguity.

In this example, certain respiratory diagnoses receive a label and everything else falls through to NULL. When you look at the output, ask whether that NULL is meaningful. Does it mean “not respiratory”? Does it mean “unknown diagnosis”? Or does it mean we forgot to define a category?

[tts-break]

Imagine a dashboard where category is displayed to users. A blank value may look like missing data rather than an intentional “other” group. In that case, an ELSE 'Other' branch might be clearer.

On the other hand, in a quality-control query, leaving unmatched values as NULL can be useful because it highlights records that need review.

The important point is to decide rather than drift into the behavior accidentally.

The same idea applies to missing input values. If a NULL bill should be labeled Needs Review, create an explicit WHEN bill_amount IS NULL branch. Do not rely on it falling through unless that is truly the intended meaning.

slides.title: Common logic traps
slides.transcript:
The most dangerous SQL logic errors are often the ones that do not produce an error message.

PostgreSQL may run the query successfully, return rows, and make the output look completely reasonable. But the rule can still be wrong.

One common trap is mixing AND and OR without parentheses. Another is using equals NULL. Another is forgetting that ordinary not-equal also becomes UNKNOWN when the field is NULL.

NOT IN can produce surprising results when the list contains NULL. CASE branches can be ordered incorrectly so a broad condition hides a specific one. Blank text can be mistaken for valid data. A zero can be confused with missingness.

[tts-break]

This is why professional SQL work includes adversarial testing. Instead of testing only normal rows, intentionally test the records most likely to break the logic.

Create or identify a row with NULL. One with zero. One with an empty string. One with only spaces. One exactly on the threshold. One that satisfies two CASE branches. One with explicit FALSE.

This is similar to testing software. Happy-path data tells you the query works in the easiest situation. Edge cases tell you whether the rule is actually reliable.

A query that “runs” is only the beginning. A query that has survived boundary testing is much closer to something you can trust.

slides.title: NOT IN with NULL
slides.transcript:
NOT IN can be surprisingly tricky when NULL appears inside the list.

Conceptually, NOT IN asks whether the value is different from every item in the list. If the list contains a NULL, SQL cannot prove that the value is different from that unknown item. The result can become UNKNOWN.

Because WHERE keeps only TRUE, rows that look like obvious non-matches may disappear.

For example, suppose we ask for payment statuses NOT IN Paid, Closed, and NULL. You may expect Open to qualify. But the presence of NULL makes the logic uncertain because SQL cannot compare Open with an unknown value in a definite way.

[tts-break]

The safe strategy is usually to keep NULL out of the IN or NOT IN list and handle missingness explicitly.

If your rule is “status is not Paid, including missing status,” write a NULL-aware condition that says exactly that. If your rule is “status is known and is not Paid,” then require IS NOT NULL along with the inequality.

This is another case where the business policy matters more than the keyword.

Whenever you see NOT IN in production SQL, especially against a subquery, ask whether the compared values can contain NULL. If they can, test carefully.

slides.title: NULL-safe inequality
slides.transcript:
This slide makes the difference between ordinary inequality and NULL-safe inequality very concrete.

Suppose we want billing records whose payment status is not Paid.

With ordinary not-equal, a known status such as Open compares cleanly with Paid and returns TRUE. But when payment status is NULL, the comparison is UNKNOWN. That row is filtered out by WHERE.

With IS DISTINCT FROM, the question changes slightly. We are asking whether the stored value is meaningfully different from Paid, including its missingness. NULL is distinct from Paid, so the row remains.

[tts-break]

Neither behavior is always correct. The right one depends on what the business question means.

If the report should show only known statuses that are not Paid, ordinary inequality may be appropriate.

If the report should show everything that is not definitely Paid, including missing statuses that need investigation, IS DISTINCT FROM is better.

This distinction appears in compliance reviews, financial reconciliation, and data-quality dashboards. Missing information often needs attention rather than silent exclusion.

Run both queries and compare the row counts. Then explain the difference in plain language. If you can explain the policy represented by each version, you understand the purpose of NULL-safe comparison.

slides.title: High-risk outreach rule
slides.transcript:
Now we combine several ideas into a more realistic cohort rule.

The patient must be active. Consent must be explicitly true. The diagnosis must be either Diabetes or Kidney Disease. Finally, the patient must have no usable email address.

Notice that each requirement represents a different kind of logic. Active status is a Boolean requirement. Consent uses explicit truth because NULL consent should not be treated as permission. Diagnosis uses membership in a target set. Email requires text normalization so NULL, empty text, and whitespace-only text all count as unusable.

All of these are connected with AND because every requirement must be satisfied.

[tts-break]

This resembles a real outreach workflow. Imagine a care-management team trying to identify people who need a phone call because they have a target chronic condition but cannot be reached by email.

The important part is that the query is explainable. We can read it as a checklist. Active? Yes. Explicit consent? Yes. Target diagnosis? Yes. Usable email absent? Yes. Then include the patient.

If Susan has the target diagnosis but consent is unknown, she should not qualify. If Robert has Kidney Disease, explicit consent, and no email, he may qualify.

A strong query lets you explain each inclusion and exclusion in business language.

slides.title: Standardized contact and billing
slides.transcript:
This report combines two different kinds of reasoning in one result.

For contact information, we normalize blank-looking text and then use COALESCE to choose the first usable contact method. That is a fallback problem.

For billing, we use CASE because we are classifying values into meaningful categories. A missing bill is labeled Needs review rather than converted to zero. An exact zero can be labeled No Charge. Then the higher billing tiers are applied using ordered thresholds.

[tts-break]

This is a good example of why NULL should not always be treated the same way across columns.

For contact information, falling back to another field may be perfectly reasonable. If email is missing but mobile phone is present, we can still create a useful display value.

For billing, a missing amount may indicate incomplete data. Replacing it with zero could falsely imply that the patient owes nothing.

The same pattern appears in business analytics. A missing product description can fall back to a short title, but a missing product price should probably not become zero. A missing office phone can fall back to mobile, but missing salary should not become zero automatically.

Use COALESCE when a fallback is semantically appropriate. Use CASE when missingness itself should produce a distinct decision or category.

slides.title: Length-of-stay categories
slides.transcript:
This example combines population filtering with classification.

The business question is about completed hospital stays, so we first remove admissions where discharge date is missing. An admission without a discharge date may still be ongoing, and it would not make sense to force it into a completed length-of-stay category.

For the remaining rows, PostgreSQL can subtract the admission date from the discharge date to calculate the number of days.

Then CASE classifies the result. Fewer than five days is Short. Five through ten days is Medium. Anything above ten days is Long.

[tts-break]

Notice the sequence. First define the population. Then calculate the measure. Then classify it.

This pattern appears in many projects. A delivery company may filter to completed deliveries before calculating delivery time. A university may filter to completed courses before classifying grade outcomes. A support team may filter to closed tickets before measuring resolution time.

Boundary testing matters here too. A stay of exactly five days should be Medium, not Short. A stay of exactly ten days is still Medium. Eleven becomes Long.

When you build duration categories, write the boundaries in plain language first. Then make sure the CASE expression matches those words exactly.

slides.title: Reproducible date rule
slides.transcript:
Time-based logic can become difficult to teach and difficult to validate when it depends on the current date.

Imagine a query that asks for admissions from the last thirty days using today's system date. If you run it this week and a student runs it next month, the result changes. That makes demonstrations, grading, and debugging harder.

For this module, we use a fixed reference date: August 11, 2026. The thirty-day window is calculated relative to that fixed point.

The query then keeps selected respiratory diagnoses and uses CASE to identify higher-risk cases when age is at least sixty.

[tts-break]

This idea of a fixed “as-of date” is very useful in real analytics too.

Financial reports often say “as of December 31.” A monthly retention report may evaluate customers as of the last day of the month. A clinical study may use a fixed index date. Machine-learning training data often needs an explicit cutoff date to prevent future information from leaking backward.

Reproducibility means someone can rerun the same logic later and get the same answer from the same data.

So when time matters, distinguish between “right now” and “as of this defined reporting date.” Both are useful, but they solve different problems.

slides.title: SQL portability
slides.transcript:
The reasoning patterns in this module transfer well across database systems, even when the exact syntax changes.

AND, OR, NOT, IS NULL, COALESCE, NULLIF, and CASE are widely supported. But some details are more platform-specific.

IS DISTINCT FROM is available in PostgreSQL and several modern systems, but not every platform handles NULL-safe comparison with the same syntax.

Date arithmetic is another common difference. PostgreSQL can subtract dates directly in many cases. SQL Server and Microsoft Fabric often use functions such as DATEDIFF. Other databases may use interval functions or date-difference functions with different argument order.

[tts-break]

The best way to move between SQL dialects is to preserve the rule before translating the syntax.

For example: “I need the number of days between admission and discharge.” That is the logic. The PostgreSQL expression is one implementation. A different platform may use another function, but the analytical meaning stays the same.

The same is true for NULL handling and CASE rules. First define the intended cohort and classifications. Then translate database-specific functions.

If you learn SQL only as memorized syntax, moving to another platform feels difficult. If you learn the reasoning, the new syntax becomes a smaller problem.

slides.title: Guided practice 1
slides.transcript:
For this guided practice, I want you to predict the result before you run the query.

We compare two versions of a mixed AND and OR rule. In the unparenthesized version, AND binds more tightly than OR. That means the consent requirement applies only to one branch of the logic.

In the parenthesized version, the age condition and the diagnosis condition are grouped together first, and then consent is required for the entire group.

Look for the patient who satisfies the age condition but has false consent. That patient is the key to understanding the difference.

[tts-break]

Do not stop at saying, “Version A returns one extra row.” Explain why.

A good explanation is: the age branch is evaluated independently of the consent test in Version A because the AND belongs to the diagnosis branch. In Version B, parentheses make consent apply to both age and diagnosis alternatives.

This is exactly how I want you to reason in real work. When two queries produce different populations, identify the record that changes and trace that record through the Boolean expression.

That is much more informative than staring at the whole result set.

slides.title: Guided practice 2
slides.transcript:
This guided practice applies our text-normalization pattern to preferred language.

The goal is not to modify the stored data. We only want to create a cleaner display value in the query output.

Start with preferred_language. Trim surrounding spaces. Then use NULLIF so that an empty cleaned value becomes NULL. Finally, use COALESCE to replace a missing result with a readable label such as Language not recorded.

[tts-break]

This distinction between stored value and derived display value is important.

In production systems, analysts often should not overwrite raw source data just to make a report prettier. Instead, they create a cleaned representation in a query, view, transformation layer, or reporting model.

That preserves traceability. We can still see what the original system stored, while users of the report get a consistent output.

The same technique works for occupation, department name, address line, product category, or any text field where blank values should be presented more clearly.

Run the query and confirm that the source value remains unchanged while the new display column contains the fallback label.

slides.title: Guided practice 3
slides.transcript:
This practice improves the billing CASE by giving an exact zero its own business meaning.

Without a special branch, zero is simply less than five thousand, so it would fall into Low-Value. But in this dataset, a zero bill represents No Charge, which is meaningfully different from a small positive charge.

The order should be deliberate. Handle NULL first as Unknown. Then handle exactly zero as No Charge. After that, apply the high and standard thresholds. ELSE can represent the remaining positive low-value bills.

[tts-break]

This is a good example of why domain meaning matters more than pure mathematics.

A zero-dollar hotel bill may mean complimentary stay. A zero inventory count may mean out of stock. A zero test score may be a real observed score. A NULL test score may mean the student never took the exam.

Technically, zero and NULL are both “not a positive amount,” but analytically they can mean very different things.

Run the query and inspect the zero-bill record. Make sure it now receives No Charge rather than Low-Value.

slides.title: Guided practice 4
slides.transcript:
This practice asks you to compare two valid but different policies.

The first filter uses ordinary not-equal. A missing payment status does not produce TRUE when compared with Paid; it produces UNKNOWN, so the row is removed.

The second filter uses IS DISTINCT FROM. That gives a definite comparison, so NULL is considered distinct from Paid and remains in the result.

The extra record is the one with missing payment status.

[tts-break]

Now translate both queries into business language.

The first means: show me records with a known status that is not Paid.

The second means: show me records that are not definitely Paid, including records whose status is missing and may need review.

Both interpretations can be correct depending on the purpose.

A collections team might want the second because missing status is a risk that requires investigation. A clean operational report might want only known non-Paid statuses.

This is the kind of choice an analyst needs to communicate. SQL should not decide the business policy for you. The query should represent a policy that was already understood.

slides.title: Guided practice 5
slides.transcript:
This guided practice changes the reference date in the recent respiratory report.

Originally, the report uses August 11, 2026. Now move the reference date to August 5, 2026 and think about how the thirty-day window changes.

Before you run the query, identify admissions near the edges of the date window. Those are the records most likely to move in or out.

Notice that changing the reference date changes the cohort, but it does not change the age threshold used by the CASE expression. The WHERE clause defines which rows are included. The CASE expression classifies the rows that survive.

[tts-break]

This separation is useful in reporting systems.

Imagine a weekly dashboard. The reporting window may move every week, while the definition of High Risk remains the same. Or the opposite may happen: the cohort stays fixed, but the classification policy changes.

When debugging a changing result, ask which part changed: population definition, calculated measure, or classification rule?

Run the revised query and compare the admissions with the original version. Focus on records near the date boundaries rather than scanning every row equally.

slides.title: Exercise 1 Boolean rule
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 1 checks whether you can translate a mixed Boolean rule correctly.

The two alternatives are age sixty-five or older, OR Kidney Disease. Those alternatives belong together. Then explicit consent must apply to the entire grouped condition.

Before writing the SQL, say the rule aloud: the patient must either be at least sixty-five or have Kidney Disease, and in either case consent must be explicitly true.

That sentence tells you where the parentheses belong.

Use the starter query and complete only the required logic. Then run the check.

If a patient with false consent appears, do not randomly change operators. Look specifically at the grouping. Ask whether consent is being applied to both alternatives or only one.

This exercise is intentionally short because the difficult part is not syntax. The difficult part is translating the policy correctly.

slides.title: Exercise 2 Contact normalization
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 2 combines text normalization with fallback logic.

Your goal is to produce the first usable contact value in this priority order: email, mobile phone, home phone, then No contact provided.

Do not use COALESCE directly on the raw fields. Remember that empty text and whitespace-only text are still non-NULL.

For each contact field, trim the text and use NULLIF to convert an empty cleaned value to NULL. Then place those normalized expressions inside COALESCE.

When you run the query, inspect the edge cases instead of only checking whether the exercise passes.

A patient with spaces in the email field should fall back to mobile. A patient with no email or mobile should use home phone. A patient with no usable contact information should receive the final label.

This exercise represents a common real-world data-preparation task: standardize first, then apply business priority.

slides.title: Exercise 3 Billing CASE
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 3 asks you to build a searched CASE with clear categories and boundaries.

Start with the exceptional states. If bill amount is NULL, return Unknown. If the amount is exactly zero, return No Charge.

Then apply the high-value threshold, followed by the standard threshold. Use ELSE for the remaining positive low-value bills.

The order matters because CASE stops at the first true branch.

After you run the query, inspect records that exercise different branches: a missing bill, a zero bill, a high-value bill, and a standard bill.

If a zero bill shows as Low-Value, the zero branch is missing or positioned incorrectly. If a missing bill becomes Low-Value, you did not handle NULL explicitly.

This is a good exercise in building a small decision tree and then testing one representative record from each branch.

slides.title: Exercise 4 NULL-safe status
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 4 is short, but it tests an important interpretation.

The wording is “not definitely Paid.” That means a missing status should remain because we cannot say that it is Paid.

Ordinary not-equal is not enough. When NULL is compared with Paid, the result is UNKNOWN and the row disappears from WHERE.

Use IS DISTINCT FROM so the comparison always produces a definite Boolean result.

After running the query, you should see the missing-status billing record included along with known non-Paid statuses.

The main lesson is to connect the operator to the wording of the policy.

“Known and not Paid” and “not definitely Paid” sound similar, but they are not the same rule. Choose the predicate that matches the intended meaning.

slides.title: Exercise 5 Length of stay
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 5 combines filtering, calculation, and classification.

First, keep only completed admissions. A completed admission has a discharge date, so use an explicit missing-value test.

Next, calculate length of stay by subtracting the admission date from the discharge date.

Then classify the result. Fewer than five days is Short. Five through ten days is Medium. More than ten days is Long.

Pay close attention to boundaries. Exactly five days should be Medium. Exactly ten days should also be Medium.

If an ongoing admission appears in your output, review the WHERE clause before changing the CASE expression. The first issue would be population selection, not classification.

This exercise reinforces a useful workflow: define the valid population first, calculate the measure second, and classify it third.

slides.title: Exercise 6 Outreach priority
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 6 brings most of the module together in one priority rule.

The highest-priority outcome is Do not contact. That applies when the record is inactive or consent is explicitly false. Put that branch first because it should override the lower-priority outcomes.

Next comes Urgent. The patient must be active, consent must be explicitly true, severity must be High, and there must be no usable email address.

Then comes Routine for active patients with explicit consent who did not already qualify as Urgent.

Everything else becomes Review.

[tts-break]

Branch order is essential. If Routine is placed before Urgent, every active consenting patient will match Routine before PostgreSQL ever reaches the Urgent branch.

The email check must also be NULL-aware. A blank or whitespace-only email should count as unavailable, not as valid contact information.

When you finish, test one example from each category. That is how you validate a multi-branch decision rule instead of trusting the syntax alone.

slides.title: Complete Module
slides.transcript:
This is the final completion step for Module 5.

The module tracks ten knowledge checks and six coding exercises, for sixteen required activities in total.

Before selecting Complete Module, review the counters and make sure they reflect the work you intended to complete. If something is missing, the page should identify the unfinished activity so you can return to that slide.

When you complete the module, the page creates a Canvas submission summary. That summary includes your knowledge-check status and the SQL saved for each coding exercise.

[tts-break]

Review the report before copying it. If the module is incomplete, the page will warn you so you know you are submitting partial progress.

Also remember that the progress is stored locally in your current browser. If you move to another computer, use a private browsing window, or clear browser storage, the saved progress may not follow you.

The purpose of this final page is not simply administrative. It is another validation step. Check that your answers, SQL, and completion status match what you actually did before you submit.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript:
Let us connect the major ideas from Module 5.

AND, OR, and NOT allow us to build compound rules. When AND and OR appear together, use parentheses so the grouping is obvious.

SQL uses three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only TRUE. This is why NULL can cause rows to disappear even when a condition is not definitely false.

NULL is not the same as zero, false, or blank text. Use IS NULL for missingness. Use Boolean predicates such as IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN when nullable Boolean fields carry distinct meanings. Use IS DISTINCT FROM when you need a definite comparison involving NULL.

[tts-break]

NULLIF is useful for normalizing values such as blank text or zero denominators. COALESCE is useful when a fallback is meaningful and documented. CASE lets us classify rows, but branch order matters because the first true branch wins.

Most importantly, validate edge cases. Test NULL, zero, blank text, whitespace, exact thresholds, explicit FALSE, and overlapping rules.

If you keep one habit from this module, make it this: write the rule in plain language before you write the SQL. Then make the SQL reflect that rule as clearly as possible.

That habit will help you in analytics, reporting, data engineering, and any project where database logic is making decisions about real records.
